message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Isotopes** | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) | Deuterium is stable; tritium is radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.3 yr). |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Weighted average of isotopes. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **Ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy to remove the single electron. |
| **Electron affinity** | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy released when an electron is added. |
| **Atomic radius** | 53 pm (covalent) | Smallest covalent radius. |
| **Molecular weight** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ (H₂) | For diatomic hydrogen gas. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) | At 1 atm. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (–434.69 °F) | At 1 atm. |
| **Density at STP** | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ | Lightest gas. |
| **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | High specific heat relative to mass. |
| **Heat of vaporization** | 0.425 kJ g⁻¹ | Low due to weak intermolecular forces. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy needed to break H₂ into atoms. |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | H₂ is a non‑polar molecule. |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive, especially as a reducing agent; forms hydrides with metals and nonmetals. | Forms H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; explosive in air (range 4–75 % H₂ in air). | Requires ignition source. |
| **Color / Odor / Taste** | Colorless, odorless, tasteless | Invisible gas. |
| **Solubility in water** | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 20 °C | Low solubility; increases slightly with pressure. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR) | Classic hydrogen emission spectrum. |
| **Role in biology** | Essential for water, organic molecules, energy metabolism (ATP). | Hydrogen bonds stabilize DNA, proteins. |
| **Industrial uses** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining, metal processing. | Clean energy potential. |
| **Safety considerations** | Explosive mixtures, cryogenic hazards (liquid H₂), tritium radioactivity. | Proper ventilation, handling protocols. |

---

### Quick Summary

- **Physical**: Lightest, colorless, odorless gas; very low boiling/melting points; high specific heat; low density.
- **Chemical**: Strong reducing agent; forms covalent bonds; participates in hydrogen bonding; highly flammable.
- **Isotopic**: Protium (stable), deuterium (stable), tritium (radioactive).
- **Applications**: Fuel cells, industrial chemistry, cryogenics, medical imaging (tritium labeling).

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
